title: Appeals Court Clears Pentagon to Flag Anthropic as National Security Threat, Politico Reports
body:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has upheld the Pentagon’s authority to deem artificial‑intelligence firm Anthropic a “national security risk” under the Defense Department’s supply‑chain risk‑management framework, a decision that preserves the government’s broad discretion to flag emerging technologies as potential threats. The ruling, issued on Thursday, affirms a lower‑court order that allowed the Department of Defense to place Anthropic on a list of vendors whose products must undergo heightened scrutiny before being used in any military system.

The panel, composed of three judges appointed by Republican presidents, issued a split opinion. Judges Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao, both selected by former President Donald Trump, joined the majority, arguing that the Pentagon’s risk‑labeling power is “rooted in longstanding statutory authority” and that the agency’s assessment of Anthropic’s large‑language model technology falls squarely within that remit. Judge Karen Henderson, a George H.W. Bush appointee, dissented, contending that the label was applied without sufficient factual basis and that it could set a dangerous precedent for overreaching governmental control over private‑sector innovation.

Anthropic, a San Francisco‑based AI startup founded by former OpenAI researchers, has attracted billions of dollars in venture funding and is known for its Claude series of conversational agents, which compete directly with ChatGPT and other large‑language models. The company’s spokesperson said the ruling “undermines legitimate commercial competition and threatens the broader AI ecosystem,” adding that Anthropic had not been provided with a clear explanation of the specific security concerns that prompted the designation. The firm has indicated it will explore further legal avenues, including a possible petition to the Supreme Court, while continuing to cooperate with the Department of Defense on non‑sensitive projects.

Legal experts note that the decision hinges on the interpretation of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which authorizes the Department of Defense to assess and mitigate supply‑chain risks that could affect the integrity of military hardware and software. The court’s majority held that the NDAA grants the Pentagon “wide latitude” to label any vendor whose products could be incorporated into defense systems, even if the perceived risk is speculative. “The judiciary is not the proper forum for second‑guessing the Pentagon’s risk assessments,” Judge Rao wrote, emphasizing deference to executive expertise in matters of national security.

Critics argue that the ruling could have chilling effects on the fast‑moving AI sector, where companies routinely share open‑source models and collaborate across borders. “When the government can unilaterally label a private firm a security risk without transparent standards, it creates uncertainty that may deter investment and slow innovation,” said Dr. Maya Patel, a professor of technology policy at Stanford University. Conversely, defense officials maintain that the measure is a prudent safeguard against potential adversarial manipulation of AI tools that could be weaponized or used to compromise classified data. “The stakes are too high to rely on voluntary compliance alone,” said a senior Pentagon official, who declined to be named.

The broader implication of the case extends beyond Anthropic. As AI technologies become increasingly integral to everything from logistics to autonomous weapons, the Pentagon is expected to expand its risk‑management program to cover a wider array of vendors, including major cloud providers and semiconductor manufacturers. The decision signals to the industry that the government will continue to wield its supply‑chain authority aggressively, potentially prompting companies to pre‑emptively adjust their architectures or seek clearer guidance from the Department of Defense.

Looking ahead, the clash between national‑security imperatives and the commercial drive for rapid AI development is likely to intensify. Lawmakers may feel pressure to clarify the criteria for “risk” designations, while firms like Anthropic will weigh the costs of legal challenges against the benefits of cooperating with defense customers. The outcome of any further appeals could set a lasting precedent for how the United States balances innovation with security in the era of generative AI.
